newsitem.title: USA: U.S. judge limits certain wood imports.
newsitem.headline: U.S. judge limits certain wood imports.

text.p: A federal judge in California has issued an order limiting imports of raw logs and other wood products into the United States because of concerns they may carry destructive pests from abroad.
U.S. District Judge Claudia Wilken in Oakland issued the preliminary injunction late last week. The decision was released on Tuesday by a coalition of environmental groups.

In the 13-page ruling, Wilken wrote that the short-term economic impact of the injunction was "outweighed by the potential for irreparable harm to American forests by the importation of exotic pests."

In a statement the environmental groups said the ruling would limit imports of raw logs and wood chips from Chile, New Zealand and Siberia, and would force the U.S. Department of Agriculture to more fully disclose the risks these imports could pose to forests in the United States.

Wilken's decision was issued in response to a lawsuit filed by several environmental groups, including the Oregon Natural Resources Council, the Pacific Environment and Resources Center, and the Western Environmental Law Center, against the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service, an agency under the Department of Agriculture.

The groups challenged the service's regulations allowing the importation of unprocessed wood products, including shiploads of raw logs and wood chips, into U.S. ports. They argued that insects and fungal pests on wood coming from other countries could decimate forests in the United States.
Wilken sided with the environmental groups, enjoining the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service from issuing any new permits for the importation of unfinished non-tropical wood products.
The injunction will remain in place until the service completes a new environmental impact study and proposes rules to regulate importation of the products.

Wilken said the environmental groups "established a substantial likelihood of irreparable harm resulting from the introduction of exotic pests into United States forests by means of imports of non-tropical unfinished wood products."

"The balance of harms tips in favor of enjoining APHIS (Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service) from issuing new permits from such products but allowing imports to continue under permits that have already been issued," she wrote.
Environmental groups said the injunction would halt the issuance of any new permits to import unprocessed wood products except tropical hardwoods and products from Canada and Mexico.
Attorneys for the Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service in Washington were not immediately available to comment on the ruling.
